article_title: Cloudflare Reclaims Another 100 Terabytes of RAM by Shrinking Its Consistent-Hashing Ring

content_preview.title: Cloudflare Reclaims Another 100 Terabytes of RAM by Shrinking Its Consistent-Hashing Ring
content_preview.summary: Cloudflare cut hash points per server by 90% and shrank its hash-point struct by 25%, freeing over 100TB of RAM on its Pingora Backend Router.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Cloudflare has freed more than 100 terabytes of RAM across its global network by rewriting how one of its core routing services distributes cacheable requests, according to a [Cloudflare Blog post](https://blog.cloudflare.com/saving-100-tb-of-ram-with-math/) published by engineers Kevin Guthrie and Mariia Iurchenko. The savings came from reworking the consistent-hashing scheme used by the Pingora Backend Router (PBR), the service that decides which server handles a given cacheable r...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean News-category structure (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis), 795 words within the 400-1200 range. Neutral, technical tone throughout with no editorializing or AI self-reference.
editor_notes.source_verification: Both sources were read in full from the gunzip'd local snapshots (not re-fetched live). source-0.html.gz (https://blog.cloudflare.com/saving-100-tb-of-ram-with-math/, sha256 3e2216ae00be3e2912bcfc3b7684640deafee79e26573fca9b9ea878df01b572, verified against manifest) and source-1.html.gz (https://blog.cloudflare.com/dns-cache-memory-optimization-1111/, sha256 ffca8bd37678f273abdb4e661ced63ad8dbca008689eb3b176a2207fb4a52b1f, verified against manifest). Both returned HTTP 200 with no archive_fallback and manifest suspicious_patterns is null for both entries -- no automated flags to independently assess. Given the extra scrutiny requested on numeric claims, every quoted figure was checked verbatim: (1) '160x625 = 100,000' hash points per server before the change -- verbatim in source-0 ('k = 160\times625 = 100{,}000'); (2) 'the last 90,000 hashes we added are buying us a minuscule 0.7% reduction in error' -- verbatim quote confirmed in source-0; (3) 'decrease the number of hashes we were generating for each server by 90% without incurring any appreciable error' -- verbatim in source-0; (4) coefficient of variation dropping from ~99% to ~8% at 160 points/server in the 100-server example -- verbatim in source-0 ('CV \approx 99%' ... 'drops from about 99% to about 8%'); (5) the 25% struct-shrink quote 'reduces the amount of memory used for consistent hashing by a whopping 25%' -- verbatim in source-0, correctly attributed to the u32-to-u16 server-index narrowing (source explicitly states the original struct is 8 bytes: 4 for the hash, 4 for the index, and that a 16-bit index suffices because PBR will not coordinate more than 2^16 (~65k) servers -- matches article's '32-bit hash alongside a 32-bit server index... narrowed to 16 bits' and 'never expected to coordinate more than roughly 65,000 servers'); (6) 'more than 100TB of RAM globally, on top of the 100TB of memory the DNS team was able to shed last month' -- verbatim in source-0; (7) rollout quotes ('PBR carried both versions of the cacheable load balancer in memory: the old ketama ring and the new smaller one', 'progressively larger groups of data centers', the traces/counters/errors/memory/startup/cache/origin-traffic list) -- all verbatim in source-0; (8) 'a (for now) unadvertised cargo feature' -- verbatim in source-0. For source-1 (DNS post): 'stores over 250 billion DNS cache entries' matches article's 'more than 250 billion entries'; 'wasting a single byte per entry costs more than 250 gigabytes of memory across our fleet' is verbatim and correctly quoted in the article's Analysis section; 'cut the per-entry footprint by over 50%' matches article's 'cutting the per-entry footprint by over 50%'; source-1's own text 'freed up roughly 100 terabytes of memory' matches article's 'shed roughly 100 terabytes of memory'. Publish dates: source-1 dated August 27, 2026; source-0 dated September 18, 2026 -- about three weeks apart, consistent with the article's framing of the DNS work as happening 'weeks earlier' / 'last month' (the latter phrase is itself a verbatim quote from source-0, not the bot's own characterization). No hallucinated quotes, no misattributed figures, no conflation between the two posts' separate percentage figures (worth confirming given extra scrutiny requested: the 90% and 25% figures are both from the PBR/consistent-hashing post, the 50%+ per-entry and 250-billion-entry figures are both from the DNS cache post -- the article keeps these correctly segregated by source). One minor completeness note: source-0 lists four bylined authors (Kevin Guthrie, Mariia Iurchenko, Zaidoon Abd Al Hadi, and Ivan Babrou) but the article names only the first two; this is an omission, not a misattribution -- the two named authors are genuinely credited on the post, so it is not inaccurate, just incomplete. Not significant enough to warrant a correction. Internal link to the earlier NGINX/Pingora retirement article (/article/2026-05/03-cloudflare-retires-15-years-of-nginx-ships-gen-13-servers-built-around-a-192-core-turin-and-a-rust-proxy) was checked against the filesystem and resolves to an existing published article.
